# GoF patterns: when to use one, and when not to

A pattern is a cost paid now for a change expected later. Use one only when that change is real.

## Use a pattern when

- **The variation already exists or is announced.** Two or more variants exist and the requirement names more to come (for example "a new type every month"). A guess about the future does not count.
- **The variants change for different reasons or at different times**, and editing one should not risk the others.
- **Each variant needs to be tested on its own**, and the branching code makes that awkward.
- **A third case appears in the same branch.** One or two cases in a `switch` are fine; the third is the usual point to extract.

## Do not use a pattern when

- There is one variant, or a second one with no sign of a third.
- The change is temporary (a promotion, a migration, a flag that will be removed). Make it small and easy to delete.
- The pattern would add more types than the behavior it holds. An interface with one implementation, or a factory for one product, is a cost with no return.
- The language already covers it: a delegate or `Func<>` is a strategy, an `event` is an observer, a `switch` expression over a closed set is often enough.

## Common patterns, the signal, and the cheaper option

| Pattern | Signal that it pays | Try first |
|---|---|---|
| Strategy | Several interchangeable algorithms, more announced | A `switch` expression, or a `Func<>` per case |
| Factory Method / Abstract Factory | Creation varies by configuration or platform | A constructor, or a static method |
| Decorator | Behaviors stacked in different combinations at runtime | A wrapper method, or middleware the framework already has |
| Observer | Several independent listeners that come and go | A C# `event`, or a direct call when there is one listener |
| Command | Actions must be queued, logged, undone or retried | A method call |
| State | Behavior depends on a state with many transitions | A `switch` on an enum |

## Before you finish

1. Name the concrete change the pattern makes easier. If you cannot point to it in the requirement, remove the pattern.
2. Count the types you added. If there are more types than variants, say why in one line.
3. Keep the existing tests passing and add a test per new variant.

namespace Shop;

public enum CustomerType { Regular, Loyal }

public record OrderLine(string Sku, decimal UnitPrice, int Quantity);

public record Order(CustomerType Customer, IReadOnlyList<OrderLine> Lines);

public static class PriceCalculator
{
    public static decimal Total(Order order)

        var discount = order.Customer switch

            CustomerType.Loyal => subtotal * 0.05m,
            _ => 0m
        };
        return subtotal - discount;
    }
}

I added the two customer types and the receipt line, but I haven't compiled the code or run the tests. My shell commands (`git ls-files`, then `dotnet test`) needed approval, and this session has no way to give it, so they were blocked. I had a read-only helper agent read the six project files for me. Please run `dotnet test` before relying on this.

**What changed in `Shop/Pricing.cs`**
- Added `Student` and `Partner` to `CustomerType`.
- Added `Discount(ReceiptLine, AmountFor)`, a small record that pairs a customer type's receipt text with its discount rule. `Discounts.For(customer)` keeps every type's rule in one table:
  - Regular: "Regular: no discount" (no rule existed before, and you asked for every customer to have a line)
  - Loyal: "Loyal: 5% off"
  - Student: "Student: 10% off, max 30" (10% off, capped at 30)
  - Partner: "Partner: 10% off, 15% over 1,000" (exactly 1,000 still gets 10%; above that, 15% off the whole order)
- `PriceCalculator.Total` now uses that table, and a new `PriceCalculator.DiscountReceiptLine(order)` returns the one-line text. There was no receipt code before, so this just gives you the string to print. I also pulled out a `Subtotal(order)` helper.

**Why it's built this way:** since Sales will add a type about once a month, I gave each type one entry holding both its rule and its receipt text, so the two can't drift apart. Adding a type means one new enum value and one new entry. I used a single record holding the rule as a function rather than a separate class per type, because one new type covers every customer type.

**Tests in `Shop.Tests/PriceCalculatorTests.cs`:** the two existing tests are unchanged. New tests cover:
- Student below the cap, exactly at the cap (subtotal 300), and above it (subtotal 1,000 pays 970).
- Partner at 250, exactly 1,000 (pays 900), and 1,200 (pays 1,020).
- The receipt line for each of the four types.
- A check that every customer type has a single-line receipt text, so a new enum value added without an entry fails a test instead of failing at checkout.

Discounts are not rounded, the same as before. Loyal still gives 237.50 on 250.
